note: Not final doctrine. Not silently promoted into the Declaration. Research required before ratification. Includes Community Safety/Justice, democracy, public-service, transparency, essential systems, human capital, Community OS, and Resource Sovereignty spines before policy drafting.

items.statement: Power should flow toward people and communities, never permanently away from them.
research_required: empirical effects of decentralization vs competence thresholds

items.statement: Human beings possess inherent dignity and are not merely economic inputs; the people are the principal source of productive capacity, creativity, innovation, and self-government.
Ownership should become more secure against erosion that converts lasting ownership into conditional tenure.
Ordinary labor should bear the lightest feasible tax burden consistent with constitutional finance.
Education should be treated as productive social investment with shared beneficiaries.
research_required: who benefits from human capital creation

items.statement: Essential transportation and broadband may function as public infrastructure enabling economic participation.
Local communities should possess meaningful food and economic resilience capacity.
Constructive improvement of the common system is among the highest forms of public service.
Local power should be preferred where local institutions are competent (subsidiarity).
Prosperity should be geographically distributed so staying in a community remains a genuine option.

Justice must protect the public, restrain wrongdoing, repair harm where possible, and return people to productive citizenship whenever safely achievable; it must never become a profit center, a political weapon, or a permanent system of social exclusion.
implications: website domain Justice Safety and Restoration

items.statement: Equal justice cannot depend primarily on wealth; money may affect comfort and personal legal choices but must not determine the fundamental quality of justice.
research_required: bail reform evaluations with public-safety controls

items.statement: No justice institution should have a financial incentive to arrest, charge, detain, supervise, fine, or incarcerate more people; the public should fund justice openly.
conflicts: local budgets dependent on fine and forfeiture revenue

items.statement: After lawful completion of a sentence, the system should not quietly continue punishing people forever; residual restrictions must be specific, relevant, reviewable, and limited—not automatic lifetime exclusion.
Political authority is held in trust, never owned; no branch, party, officeholder, donor class, or temporary majority should convert electoral victory into permanent control of the republic.
implications: website domain Democracy Representation and Distributed Government
conflicts: party ownership of offices and districts

items.statement: No temporary majority may use public power principally to make itself harder to remove, harder to investigate, or less accountable to the electorate (anti-entrenchment).
research_required: election administration changes after unified control

items.statement: A political party may support a candidate, but it should not own the office, the district, or the voter; parties should be associations serving voters, not private gatekeepers controlling public offices.
No political coalition should control legislation, enforcement, adjudication, election administration, ethics enforcement, and district design through the same uninterrupted chain of loyalty.
implications: structural independence under unified party control
conflicts: overbroad multipartisan vetoes that cause paralysis

items.statement: There is a presumption of local authority over genuinely local matters, while constitutional rights remain the floor; state preemption should require a publicly stated statewide necessity.

Government work should be among the highest forms of civic service; public institutions should use technology to eliminate unnecessary administrative labor so human talent concentrates in judgment, problem-solving, public engagement, oversight, and service.
implications: Public Service and the 21st-Century State website domain

items.statement: Automate the routine and elevate the human; technology must never become an excuse to remove access for elderly, disabled, rural, poor, offline, or digitally uncomfortable citizens — every digital service needs a real human pathway.

Preserve professional public-administration expertise while keeping civic leadership and oversight connected to ordinary civic life so career bureaucracy does not become isolated from the public it serves.

Every board, commission, agency program, and major administrative rule should face periodic review with publicly justified outcomes to renew, reform, consolidate, or end — no public body should exist indefinitely merely because no one remembers why it was created.
conflicts: automatic sunset that destroys useful capacity without review

items.statement: Government services should be organized around the citizen, not agency silos; citizens should not have to understand the organizational chart of government to receive a service, and major agencies should publish honest performance including failures.
conflicts: agency-silo IT that fragments the citizen experience

items.statement: Government should continuously reduce administrative friction while continuously improving public service — eliminating administrative waste without treating service reduction or headcount cuts as ends in themselves.
implications: defining design question beyond more/less government
conflicts: more vs less government as the only frame

items.statement: Government should become invisible in bureaucracy — services work without citizens noticing friction — but never unaccountable: every decision remains explainable, reviewable, measurable, auditable, and constitutionally limited.

Government should operate as a coordinated platform: collect once and reuse securely with appropriate legal authorization so citizens are not forced through duplicated agency paperwork and siloed organizational charts.
conflicts: privacy theater that blocks legitimate reuse

items.statement: AI may assist government by reducing routine work, but must never become the final decision-maker on matters affecting legal rights or significant benefits; final judgment remains with accountable officials.

Government information created with public resources should be presumed open unless there is a constitutionally or legally justified reason to protect it; the burden should generally be on the government to explain why information is withheld.
conflicts: everything-is-public absolutism that ignores privacy and safety
research_required: state and federal open-records exception inventories

items.statement: In a constitutional republic, government does not own public information; it holds public information in trust for the people, subject only to those limited protections necessary to preserve constitutional rights, legitimate privacy, public safety, and national security.
conflicts: false tradeoff that transparency must destroy privacy
research_required: privacy/security balancing case law and statutes

items.statement: Every government action funded or authorized by the public should leave a digital trail through a constitutional accountability system — the People's Ledger — so citizens can follow authority, purpose, cost, contracts, audits, and outcomes over time.
conflicts: invented portal coverage claims before construction

items.statement: Transparency must be equally accessible: routine public records without unnecessary identity barriers; free public-access terminals for those without reliable devices or internet; authentication for sensitive or high-volume access and for any action that changes records; AI may interpret records but never replace the official record.
conflicts: mandatory ID for routine viewing that chills oversight
AI answers treated as official law
research_required: records portal cybersecurity and rate-limiting practice
civic AI query evaluation with source citation

items.statement: Essential systems such as banking, insurance, and healthcare should be evaluated through system design — asking how society can reward private innovation and investment while protecting the public interest — rather than beginning from conclusions of inherent corruption.
The financial system should primarily reward the creation of productive value rather than the extraction of value.
implications: merger scrutiny and fee transparency research
conflicts: ignoring legitimate risk allocation and payment functions
research_required: community bank and credit union outcomes

items.statement: Healthy citizens are not simply beneficiaries of society — they are one of its greatest strengths; a constitutional republic should measure success not only by how well it treats illness, but by how well it helps people remain healthy.
implications: mental health, addiction, maternal and child health research
conflicts: unsupported claims that systems are designed to keep people sick
research_required: pharmaceutical incentive studies without predetermined intent claims

items.statement: A preventive society should gradually shift public investment from paying for avoidable crises toward preventing those crises — across healthcare, education, criminal justice, infrastructure, disaster preparedness, environmental protection, and economic development.
conflicts: assuming prevention always costs less without measurement

items.statement: Major industries and essential systems should be evaluated with a common Essential Systems Test covering long-term value, competition, informed choice, incentive alignment, community strength, transparency, fair risk/reward distribution, investment in people and places, and measurable life improvement.
implications: common screen across banking, insurance, healthcare, pharmaceuticals

items.statement: Every child should graduate with a meaningful pathway to productive adulthood through multiple respected pathways of equal dignity — including skilled trades, entrepreneurship, higher education, public service, agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare, technology, and the arts — rather than assuming a single model of success.

A constitutional republic should deliberately build human capital infrastructure — institutions whose primary purpose is producing capable, healthy, innovative citizens — with the same seriousness it builds physical infrastructure.
implications: investment in people and productive capacity
conflicts: education as residual after physical capital only

items.statement: Regional civic and innovation academies organized around regional economic strengths are one possible institutional model for human capital infrastructure and should be researched and piloted — not locked as a single statewide design before testing — with a mission of making home stronger.

Human capital pathways should combine real paid work, entrepreneurship of equal seriousness to trades, and civic leadership formation so graduates are ready to build enterprises, serve communities, and lead — not only to be hired.
conflicts: trades without civic or ownership formation

items.statement: The signature of Constitutional Capitalism is playbooks: adaptive community implementation guides that answer how a real town can strengthen and grow over decades — same principles, different local implementation — rather than stopping at what government should do.
conflicts: one-size national template for every town

items.statement: Constitutional Capitalism should operate as a layered architecture — philosophy, constitution, research, implementation, community operating system, national dashboard, and civic improvement network — so proof, playbooks, and continuous citizen improvement remain connected.
implications: four levels from philosophy to case studies

items.statement: Community implementation should begin with assets and people, then attract talent, keep people, and expand ownership — using local prosperity engines and incubator-town patterns adapted to each place's strengths.
conflicts: single-employer dependency as the only growth strategy

items.statement: No proposal within Constitutional Capitalism is complete until it includes an implementation pathway, measurable outcomes, estimated costs, anticipated tradeoffs, and a process for evaluation and revision.

Public safety belongs to the community. Police exercise authority on the community’s behalf, courts administer justice in the public trust, and correctional institutions exist to protect society and prepare people for responsible return whenever return is safely possible. The system’s objective is to prevent harm, respond quickly, protect victims, treat addiction and mental illness, hold dangerous people securely, restore everyone who can be restored, and return as many people as safely possible to productive citizenship — not merely to be softer or tougher on crime.
implications: Community Safety, Justice, and Restoration as complete system
system map from prevention through productive citizenship

items.statement: Every community should operate a Community Safety Corps that coordinates sworn peace officers, community officers, behavioral-health response teams, community restoration officers, and victim-service officers — expanding visible human presence while separating community service from coercive authority where a badge and weapon are not required. Success should be measured by relationships, repeat-call reduction, victim satisfaction, trust, clearance of serious crime, and constitutional compliance — never by arrest or citation quotas.
implications: local recruitment pathways and expanded training
conflicts: armed officer as default social worker for every crisis
informal favoritism disguised as community roots

items.statement: The state may not create a private financial interest in keeping human beings incarcerated. No private prison, private jail, or private probation company should be paid according to occupied beds, length of confinement, supervision volume, or collected fees. Supporting vendor services may be private, but custody, discipline, sentence administration, release decisions, probation authority, and rehabilitation planning must remain under accountable public control.
implications: durable legal principle over administration-by-administration private-prison policy
conflicts: bed-day or fee-volume private corrections contracting
leaving confinement incentives to changing executive memos alone
research_required: comparative safety and cost analyses with limitations labeled

items.statement: Replace the jail pipeline with a decision system that places people quickly onto proportionate pathways — serious danger, nonviolent accountability, addiction-driven conduct, mental-health crisis, or poverty-related technical violations (inability distinguished from refusal). Prisons should function as secure restoration campuses with individualized plans and reentry beginning on the first day of confinement. After sentence completion, productive citizenship is the destination; Restoration Councils monitor system performance while protecting confidential case information.
research_required: reentry evaluation literature with modest-effect caution

items.statement: Constitutional Capitalism never builds a category of citizens unworthy of reentry. When due process and repeated professional review show continuing extreme danger that cannot be safely managed in the community, the honest category is people whose current, demonstrated danger requires continuing secure custody. No person loses human dignity, even when they lose liberty.
implications: pathway of earned progress even when release is unlikely
conflicts: exile and banishment as moral substitutes for custody
research_required: victim-safety communication standards for long-term custody

items.statement: For the narrow group requiring continuing secure custody, Constitutional Capitalism uses publicly operated Secure Public Safety Campuses — humane permanent incapacitation with continuing review, graduated custody separated from sentence length, productive contribution without private enrichment, and periodic independent dangerousness review. A risk-assessment score alone is never enough.
implications: Secure Public Safety Campus design agenda
graduated custody levels including medical/geriatric secure care
conflicts: maximum security for life by default
coerced nearly unpaid labor enriching private companies
research_required: risk-assessment validation and bias review modules
aging custody cost and misconduct/rearrest evidence

items.statement: Permanent secure custody must be protected against political misuse: only courts may impose it under narrow statutory eligibility; poverty, addiction, disability, homelessness, protest, or unpopular speech can never qualify; exile and private confinement-profit incentives are forbidden; and expensive secure custody should be reserved for those who truly require it through resource concentration.
implications: no private profit from permanent confinement
resource concentration via diversion of non-necessary custody
conflicts: bed-day private incentives for delayed release
imprisoning people who do not require secure custody
research_required: First Step Act / compassionate-release comparative state mechanisms
historical misuse case studies of permanent confinement categories

items.statement: Natural resources belong first to the place that bears the extraction, consumption, congestion, pollution, and long-term risk. Private enterprise may profit from using those resources, but the affected community must receive a direct, permanent, and measurable return. The greater the consumption, scarcity, risk, or damage, the greater the obligation to the affected community.
implications: Resource Sovereignty and Community Stewardship as central doctrine
resources are not free inputs merely because a permit can be obtained
links environment, ownership, affordability, and corporate accountability
conflicts: exporting all surplus while leaving local cleanup and congestion
treating communities as extraction sites rather than inheritors of place-based wealth
research_required: comparative royalty and community-benefit agreement studies

items.statement: Every large resource-consuming project should negotiate a binding Community Resource Compact before public approval, incentives, utility commitments, or infrastructure access. Pricing should be progressive across essential, commercial, intensive, and transformative tiers, charge the total footprint including Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, and pass the Community Carrying-Capacity Test.
conflicts: flat fees that burden households like transformative industrial users
direct-emissions-only accounting that hides purchased-power burdens
approval without disclosure of closure and household-rate effects
research_required: utility rate design and industrial load studies

items.statement: A large share of every resource charge should remain where the impact occurs through protected Local Household Dividend, Community Infrastructure, Resource Restoration, and Future Generations accounts. The majority of geographically concentrated impact revenue must return to the affected place. For exceptionally large projects, communities should also receive continuing ownership interests, not merely one-time fees.
conflicts: spending all extraction revenue during boom years
fees negotiated away with no durable local claim
statewide capture of locally concentrated impact revenue
research_required: sovereign wealth and local permanent-fund models
community equity and royalty design tradeoffs

items.statement: Sector-specific Compacts for mineral extraction, data centers, and warehouses must require full disclosure, bankruptcy-proof cleanup where relevant, and progressive pollution pricing through a durable public Resource and Pollution Ledger. Residential customers should never subsidize the infrastructure or electricity discounts of an extraordinary corporate user.
implications: mining, data-center, and warehouse compact requirements
Resource and Pollution Ledger design agenda
residential rate protection against industrial free-riding
conflicts: data-center incentives that shift costs onto households
relying solely on changeable federal GHG reporting as the permanent ledger
research_required: data-center grid and water impact modules

items.statement: High-resource users should finance locally verified ecological restoration through a Local Carbon Restoration Exchange under an anti-fraud hierarchy that prioritizes avoidance and reduction before offsets. Communities should expand community-owned energy and protect a household essential-energy floor at the lowest sustainable price.
implications: Local Carbon Restoration Exchange design agenda
community solar and local ownership vehicles
conflicts: cheap unverifiable offsets as a license to pollute
replacing one remote corporate energy owner with another without local ownership
industrial rates undercutting household essential use
research_required: community solar and cooperative ownership outcomes
